chapter: Learning piano, dancing and Alphonso Trent
title: Dancing with Alphonso Trent's band at white hotels
summary: Trent's manager Bud Goldberg takes the Charleston dancer along to hotel dates, paying him and letting him sit behind the piano.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Was real strict, you know, the eighth note, hit your hand...why didn't you see that accidental, that's an eighth note, that's a B-flat, and so forth. But she said that to me. And then I paid attention to that. But Bud Goldberg, who was the manager of Alphonso Trent's orchestra, came up to a dance in the black community with Trent. And he saw me out on the floor dancing, and everybody was crowded around me, you know, when you're a crowd-seeker, you know, and he said to Trent, "Why don't we take that dancer and let him dance with the band, you know, when they play the Adolphus Hotel or some big places, you know, white people they want to see a black kid dancing." And I could really do the Charleston. The Charleston had become a rage across America and really, if you could do the Charleston you were it in those days, and do it well. So they decided that I would go like to Mineral Wells or Austin or Houston or wherever they'd go. And they didn't allow...I could go in with the band and sit behind the piano until the time come for me to come out and do my Charleston. The band would pay

me and then I'd get a lot of tips. So this is how I really broke into like what I call the big time. But one of the things that happened was, that sitting behind that piano for three or four hours, I had an opportunity to really listen at changes--hearing a guy play a different kind of thing, or hear now the trumpets coming in, or the piano would be playing--this is a piano solo or clarinet solo, so I had an opportunity during the period that I was with Trent to know these things, which didn't hurt.
